stem: For the reaction \(\mathrm{2\,N_2O_5(g) \longrightarrow 4\,NO_2(g) + O_2(g)}\) in liquid bromine, \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) disappears at a rate of \(0.02\) moles \(\mathrm{dm^{-3}\ sec^{-1}}\). At what rate \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) are formed? What would be the rate of reaction?
solution:
Given : \(-\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{dt} = 0.02\)

i. Rate of reaction

\(= -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{dt} = \dfrac{d[\mathrm{O_2}]}{dt}\)

\(= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{dt}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.02 = 0.01\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\)

ii. Rate of formation of \(\mathrm{O_2} = \dfrac{d[\mathrm{O_2}]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(-\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{dt}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 0.02\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}} = 0.01\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\)

iii. Rate of formation of \(\mathrm{NO_2} = \dfrac{d[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{dt} = \dfrac{4}{2}\left(-\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{dt}\right) = 2 \times 0.02\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}} = 0.04\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\)

subtopic: Rate of Reaction and Reactant Concentration
stem:
Write the rate law for the reaction, \(\mathrm{A + B \longrightarrow P}\) from the following data :

| [A] mol dm\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\) (Initial) | [B] mol dm\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\) (Initial) | Initial rate mol dm\(^{-3}\) s\(^{-1}\) |
|---|---|---|
| (i) 0.4 | 0.2 | \(4.0 \times 10^{-5}\) |
| (ii) 0.6 | 0.2 | \(6.0 \times 10^{-5}\) |
| (iii) 0.8 | 0.4 | \(3.2 \times 10^{-4}\) |
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the data table heads its two concentration columns \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\), but a concentration cannot carry \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\); the correct unit for both is \(\mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\). Only the third column, the initial rate, is per second. The answer is unaffected, because the derivation uses only the ratios of the tabulated values.]

Rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\)

a. From above data (i) and (ii), when \([\mathrm{A}]\) increases by a factor \(1.5\) keeping \([\mathrm{B}]\) as constant, the rate increases by a factor \(1.5\). It means rate \(\propto [\mathrm{A}]\) and \(x = 1\)

b. From observations (i) and (iii), it can be seen that when concentrations of A and B are doubled, the rate increases by a factor \(8\). Due to doubling of \([\mathrm{A}]\) the rate is doubled (because \(x = 1\)) that is rate increases by a factor \(2\).

This implies that doubling \([\mathrm{B}]\), the rate increases by a factor \(4\), or rate \(\propto [\mathrm{B}]^2\) and \(y = 2\). Therefore, rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2\)

**Alternatively**

The rate law gives rate \(= k\,[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\).

a. From above observations (i) and (ii)

(i) \(4 \times 10^{-5} = (0.4)^x(0.2)^y\)

(ii) \(6 \times 10^{-5} = (0.6)^x(0.2)^y\)

Dividing (ii) by (i), we have

\(\dfrac{6 \times 10^{-5}}{4 \times 10^{-5}} = 1.5 = \dfrac{(0.6)^x(0.2)^y}{(0.4)^x(0.2)^y} = \left(\dfrac{0.6}{0.4}\right)^x = (1.5)^x\)

Hence \(x = 1\)

b. From observations (i) and (iii) separately in the rate law gives

(iii) \(4 \times 10^{-5} = (0.4) \times (0.2)^y\) since \(x = 1\)

(iv) \(3.2 \times 10^{-4} = 0.8 \times (0.4)^y\)

Dividing (iv) by (iii) we write

\(\dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-4}}{4 \times 10^{-5}} = \dfrac{0.8\,(0.4)^y}{0.4\,(0.2)^y}\)

or \(8 = 2 \times \left(\dfrac{0.4}{0.2}\right)^y\)

or \(4 = 2^2 = 2^y\)

Therefore \(y = 2\).

The rate law is then rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2\).

subtopic: Rate of Reaction and Reactant Concentration
stem: For the reaction, \(\mathrm{2\,NOBr(g) \longrightarrow 2\,NO(g) + Br_2(g)}\), the rate law is rate \(= k[\mathrm{NOBr}]^2\). If the rate of the reaction is \(6.5 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) when the concentration of \(\mathrm{NOBr}\) is \(2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\). What would be the rate constant for the reaction?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book prints the final unit as \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\), which contradicts its own substitution one line above — \((\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}) / (\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^2\) gives \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\), with \(L\) to the power \(+1\). The unit has been corrected here so the worked example does not teach the wrong dimensions for a second order rate constant; the value \(1.625\) is as printed and is correct.]

rate \(= k[\mathrm{NOBr}]^2\)  or  \(k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{NOBr}]^2}\)

\(= \dfrac{6.5 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}s^{-1}}}{(2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}})^2}\)

\(= 1.625\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}\ L\ s^{-1}}\)

subtopic: Rate of Reaction and Reactant Concentration
stem: For the reaction \(\mathrm{2NO(g) + 2H_2(g) \longrightarrow N_2(g) + 2\,H_2O(g)}\), the rate law is rate \(= k[\mathrm{NO}]^2[\mathrm{H_2}]\). What is the order with respect to \(\mathrm{NO}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2}\)? What is the overall order of the reaction?
solution: In the rate law expression, the exponent of \([\mathrm{NO}]\) is \(2\) and that of \([\mathrm{H_2}]\) is \(1\). Hence, reaction is second order in \(\mathrm{NO}\), first order in \(\mathrm{H_2}\) and the reaction is third order.

subtopic: Rate of Reaction and Reactant Concentration
stem: The rate of the reaction, \(\mathrm{A + B \longrightarrow P}\) is \(3.6 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}\ s^{-1}}\) when \([\mathrm{A}] = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) and \([\mathrm{B}] = 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\). Calculate the rate constant if the reaction is first order in A and second order in B.
solution:
The reaction is first order in A and second order in B. Hence, the rate law gives

rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2\)  or  \(k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2}\)

rate \(= 3.6 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}s^{-1}}\), \([\mathrm{A}] = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\) and \([\mathrm{B}] = 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

Substitution gives

\(k = \dfrac{3.6 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}s^{-1}}}{0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}} \times (0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}})^2}\)

\(= \dfrac{3.6 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{0.2 \times 0.01\ \mathrm{mol^2\ dm^{-6}\ s^{-1}}}\)

\(= 18\ \mathrm{mol^{-2}\ dm^{6}\ s^{-1}}\)

subtopic: Rate of Reaction and Reactant Concentration
stem: Consider, \(\mathrm{A + B \longrightarrow P}\). If the concentration of A is doubled with \([\mathrm{B}]\) being constant, the rate of the reaction doubles. If the concentration of A is tripled and that of B is doubled, the rate increases by a factor \(6\). What is order of the reaction with respect to each reactant? Determine the overall order of the reaction.
solution:
Rate of reaction : rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\) …… (i)

If \([\mathrm{A}]\) is doubled, the rate doubles.

\(\therefore\ 2 \times \text{rate} = k\,[2\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y = k\,2^x\,[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y\) …… (ii)

\(6 \times \text{rate} = k\,[3\mathrm{A}]^x[2\mathrm{B}]^y\) …… (iii)

\(\dfrac{\text{(ii)}}{\text{(i)}}\) gives \(\dfrac{2 \times \text{rate}}{\text{rate}} = \dfrac{k\,2^x[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y}{k\,[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y}\)

\(\dfrac{\text{(iii)}}{\text{(i)}}\) gives \(\dfrac{6 \times \text{rate}}{\text{rate}} = \dfrac{3^x k[\mathrm{A}]^x 2^y[\mathrm{B}]^y}{k\,[\mathrm{A}]^x[\mathrm{B}]^y} = 3^x \times 2^y\)

substitute \(x = 1\)

\(\therefore\ 6 = 3 \times 2^y\) or \(2 = 2^y\) and \(y = 1\)

The reaction is first order in A and first order in B. The overall reaction is of the second order.

stem:
A reaction occurs in the following steps

i. \(\mathrm{NO_2(g) + F_2(g) \longrightarrow NO_2F(g) + F(g)}\) (slow)

ii. \(\mathrm{F(g) + NO_2(g) \longrightarrow NO_2F(g)}\) (fast)

a. Write the equation of overall reaction.

b. Write down rate law.

c. Identify the reaction intermediate.
solution:
a. The addition of two steps gives the overall reaction as

\(\mathrm{2NO_2(g) + F_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,NO_2F(g)}\)

b. Step (i) is slow. The rate law of the reaction is predicted from its stoichiometry. Thus,

rate \(= k[\mathrm{NO_2}]\,[\mathrm{F_2}]\)

c. F is produced in step (i) and consumed in step (ii) or F is the reaction intermediate.

stem: The half life of first order reaction is \(990\ \mathrm{s}\). If the initial concentration of the reactant is \(0.08\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\), what concentration would remain after \(35\) minutes?
In a first order reaction \(60\%\) of the reactant decomposes in \(45\) minutes. Calculate the half life for the reaction.

Following data were obtained during the first order decomposition of \(\mathrm{SO_2Cl_2}\) at the constant volume.

\(\mathrm{SO_2Cl_2(g) \longrightarrow SO_2(g) + Cl_2(g)}\)

| Times/s | Total pressure/bar |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.5 |
| 100 | 0.6 |

Calculate the rate constant of the reaction.
The rate constants for a first order reaction are \(0.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\) at \(313\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(0.045\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\) at \(293\ \mathrm{K}\). What is the activation energy?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the last line prints the units as \(\mathrm{J/mol^{-1}}\) and \(\mathrm{kJ/mol^{-1}}\), which invert "per mole" twice; they should read \(\mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) (equivalently \(\mathrm{J/mol}\) and \(\mathrm{kJ/mol}\)). The numerical result \(98.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) is correct.]

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)\)

\(k_1 = 0.045\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(k_2 = 0.6\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\), \(T_1 = 293\ \mathrm{K}\), \(T_2 = 313\ \mathrm{K}\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\)

Substituting

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{0.6}{0.045} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \left[\dfrac{313 - 293}{293 \times 313}\right]\)

\(\log_{10} 13.33 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{20}{293 \times 313}\)

\(1.1248 = \dfrac{E_a}{19.15} \times 2.18 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(E_a = 1.1248 \times 19.15\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}} / 2.18 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(= 98810\ \mathrm{J/mol^{-1}} = 98.8\ \mathrm{kJ/mol^{-1}}\)

stem: A first order gas phase reaction has activation energy of \(240\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). If the pre-exponential factor is \(1.6 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). what is the rate constant of the reaction at \(600\ \mathrm{K}\)?
solution:
Arrhenius equation

\(k = \mathrm{A}\,e^{-E_a/RT}\) is written as

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,RT}\)

\(E_a = 240\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} = 240 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\),

\(T = 600\ \mathrm{K}\), \(\mathrm{A} = 1.6 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

Hence \(\log_{10}\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \dfrac{240 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}\ K^{-1}} \times 600\ \mathrm{K}} = 20.89\)

\(\dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{k} = \text{antilog } 20.89 = 7.78 \times 10^{20}\)

and \(k = \dfrac{\mathrm{A}}{7.78 \times 10^{20}} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{7.78 \times 10^{20}} = 2.055 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

stem: The half life of a first order reaction is \(900\) min at \(820\ \mathrm{K}\). Estimate its half life at \(720\ \mathrm{K}\) if the activation energy is \(250\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book writes the temperature-dependence relation with \(2.303\,RT\) in the denominator, where \(2.303\,R\) belongs — the temperature is already carried by the bracket \((T_2 - T_1)/T_1T_2\). The chapter's own Eq. (6.23) prints \(E_a/(2.303\,R)\), and this example's own substitution divides by \(2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\) with no \(T\), which is what gives its printed \(2.212\). The formula has been corrected here; the printed answer \(1.464 \times 10^{5}\) min is correct.]

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

Rate constants at two different temperatures, \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) are \(k_1\) and \(k_2\) respectively, and the corresponding half lives \((t_{1/2})_1\) and \((t_{1/2})_2\).

\((t_{1/2})_1 = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\) and \((t_{1/2})_2 = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)

Hence, \(\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \dfrac{k_2}{k_1}\)

The equation, \(\log_{10}\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R} \times \left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right]\)

\(\log_{10}\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right]\)

\(E_a = 250\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), \(T_1 = 720\ \mathrm{K}\),

\(T_2 = 820\ \mathrm{K}\), \((t_{1/2})_2 = 900\) min

Thus, \(\log_{10}\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \dfrac{250 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}}{2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}mol^{-1}}}\left[\dfrac{820\ \mathrm{K} - 720\ \mathrm{K}}{820\ \mathrm{K} \times 720\ \mathrm{K}}\right] = 2.212\)

\(\dfrac{(t_{1/2})_1}{(t_{1/2})_2} = \text{antilog } 2.212 = 162.7\)

\((t_{1/2})_1 = (t_{1/2})_2 \times 162.7 = 900 \times 162.7 = 1.464 \times 10^{5}\) min
